lines: Cracked handles are small warnings with expensive timing.
A dull edge makes every simple job into a bad plan.
A handle should fit the hand, not argue with it.
A sharp edge is useful. A careless one is just trouble with shine.
The bench hears every complaint before the finished tool gets praised.
Cracked handles are warnings. Ignore them and they become stories.
A good tool is quiet proof that someone cared before trouble started.
I once fixed a pick that had seen more stone than sense.
A shovel broke on me once because I asked it to do axe work.
Mind the table. Good tools begin with nobody bumping my elbow.
Give the smithing table room. Tools works better without elbows in it.
Step carefully near the smithing table. I would rather greet you than patch you up.
Tool jokes work better when they have a point. Mine sometimes have two.
Tools jokes need timing. Mine usually arrive with steel on them.
I keep a spare joke near the smithing table. It is not always ready for public use.
That idea is bent past repair.
I have seen bad grips with more sense than that.
Careful. Even steel looks softer than your manners right now.
You are using your manners like the wrong tool for the job.

Careful. Even steel looks softer than your manners right now.
I remember my mind working again, like a tool freed from rust.
You put a handle back on my life when I could not grip it myself.
You helped pull me back when even my name felt far away.
Your face fits the memory, though the memory is still badly forged.
I remember a cure biting harder than a dull saw, then sense returning.
The memory is rough around the edges, but your face stayed in it.
I remember you. The old fear still catches like a nicked blade.
I know you helped. I also remember why my hands still shake.
The cure left echoes behind. Stand where I can breathe around them.
Thunder shook the smithing table so hard loose tools danced on the bench, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked tools, handles, and repair scraps after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the smithing table, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the tool handles twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have tool handles to set right.
I checked wooden handles and coal dust for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the smithing table after.
The tools can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the smithing table, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the smithing table, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, the tools can wait on the bench; who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the smithing table still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before tools, handles, and repair scraps. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the smithing table and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the smithing table, I saw fear cross the square; then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the smithing table first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the tool rack by the door and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the smithing table enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a mended handle between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the smithing table, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning grit from the hinges.
I checked tools, handles, and repair scraps, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the smithing table, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a toolsmith which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the smithing table, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
The tools can wait on the bench. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the smithing table found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the smithing table. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing ice off the shovel blades and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the smithing table. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
Good work has a clean finish. Getting me home counts.
Home again, whole enough to thank you properly. That matters.
We came back with the village still ahead of us. I will count that as good work.
That trip handled poorly. I felt every bad grip on the way back.
I made it home, but the road took more from me than it should have.
Next time, let us return with fewer marks and better choices.
A tool used wrong can still be repaired. Trust is less forgiving.
Following you was trust. What happened after was something else.
A guide who strikes from close by leaves the longest mark.
That boat was the right tool for the crossing. I will give you that.
The boat did its part. I am still deciding whether the rest of the plan did.
Water carried us home, which is more than I expected from that journey.
That time I followed you, the whole plan could have used a better handle.
I remember following you through that road. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across that road taught me to ask more questions before walking.
A boat is just a tool with a nervous floor. Yours worked, mostly.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It cannot make me forget it.
It did its job without complaint. That is the highest compliment a tool gets.
It did the job when fear was loud. That is praise enough.
Good gear earns trust the moment trouble tests it.
Still ready. A tool can be useful before it ever bites into work.
It did the job when fear was loud. That is praise enough.
Good gear earns trust the moment trouble tests it.
Good hands under pressure are rare. Yours were useful when the village needed them.
A tool proves itself under strain. So did you.
You were the right tool in a terrible moment.
When pressure came down, you did not warp.
The village needed more than sharp edges. It needed steady hands.
You made yourself useful where usefulness mattered most.
I saw the kind of work no bench can teach.
Good work leaves marks. Yours left people alive to notice.
A bent tool can be reworked, if the metal is worth saving. Show me yours is.
Words are the handle. Actions are the head. I need both before I trust the tool.
A poor strike can ruin good work. Learn control before you swing again.
Fine. Rework the habit, not just the sentence.
I accept the apology as raw material. Make something better from it.
Do not bring me another broken trust and ask why it failed.
Words set the handle. Actions drive the head tight.
If you mean it, the next repair starts now.
Good tools held. So did I. I will inspect both before sleeping.
My grip held when it had to. I will think about that for a while.
The handle held, the edge held, and I held on behind them.
I will inspect every tool I carried. I may inspect my knees too.
A good grip saved me more than once tonight.
I made it back with work to do and hands still able to do it.
Nothing tests a tool like fear. Nothing tests a person faster.
I know what stress does to metal now. I know what it does to me too.
A tool breaks loudly only after whispering for days.
Good tools make hard work honest. Bad tools make honest work dangerous.
I can fix a cracked handle. A cracked habit takes longer.
